intro: Two schools argue about hundreds of rules. A heavenly voice takes a side, and the rabbis politely say no. A great teacher leaves the path, and his student keeps learning from him anyway. These are some of the most famous passages in the Talmud. In this unit you will read them in paraphrase and follow how they move.

The unit has two threads. The first is argument: how the rabbis disagreed, who decided, and why they kept the losing side on the page. The second is mercy: how the Talmud's stories and sayings protect people from shame, gossip and harsh judgment.

By the end you will be able to explain Eruvin 13b and Bava Metzia 59b in your own words. You will be able to quote Pirkei Avot and say who said what. And you will be able to show how Jewish readers, from traditional to academic, have read these texts differently.
bigQuestion: How can people argue hard and still treat each other with mercy?

timeline.t: Hillel and Shammai teach in Jerusalem
Rome destroys the Temple in Jerusalem
Rabbis at Yavneh follow Beit Hillel, as the Talmud tells it
Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Joshua; the oven debate, as the story sets it
Rabbi Tarfon and Ben Zoma teach
Elisha ben Abuyah and his student Rabbi Meir
The Mishnah, including Pirkei Avot, is edited
The Babylonian Talmud takes its final shape
Charles Taylor publishes his English Avot
The Chafetz Chaim, teacher of kind speech, dies

words.d: the House of Hillel, the school whose rulings the law usually follows
the House of Shammai, usually the stricter school
a heavenly voice, in rabbinic stories
the larger number; the rabbis decided law by majority vote
a view that lost the vote but is kept in the text
the Talmud's stories and ethical teachings
Chapters of the Fathers, a tractate of ethical sayings
true but harmful talk about another person
returning; turning away from a wrong
the Other; the Talmud's name for Elisha ben Abuyah
doing more than the strict rule requires

test.q: Why does the law usually follow Beit Hillel, according to Eruvin 13b?
choices: they were kind and taught Beit Shammai's view before their own
test.why: Eruvin 13b says both are the words of the living God, but Beit Hillel were humble and taught the other view first.

test.q: In the Oven of Akhnai story, what does Rabbi Joshua answer to the heavenly voice?
test.why: Rabbi Joshua cites Deuteronomy 30:12 in Bava Metzia 59b.

test.q: Where is the Oven of Akhnai story told?
test.why: The story is in the Babylonian Talmud, Bava Metzia 59b.

choices: the Talmud's stories and ethical teachings
test.why: Aggadah is the non-legal part of rabbinic literature.

test.q: What does Avot 5 call a dispute that lasts?
choices: one for the sake of heaven
test.why: Avot 5:17 (5:20 in some editions) says a dispute for the sake of heaven will endure.

test.q: Who said 'If I am only for myself, what am I?'
What does Ben Zoma say makes a person wise?
test.why: Ben Zoma says this in Avot 4:1.

test.q: What does the Mishnah Yoma 8:9 teach about wrongs between people?
choices: you must make peace with the person you hurt
test.why: Yom Kippur does not atone for them until the person makes peace.

test.q: Why does the Talmud keep minority opinions like Rabbi Eliezer's?
choices: so later courts and readers can learn from them
test.why: The Mishnah (Eduyot 1:5) explains that minority views are recorded for later use.
Bava Metzia 58b discusses wronging with words.

test.q: How did Rabbi Meir treat his teacher Elisha ben Abuyah?
choices: he refused to speak to him
he kept the teaching and left the rest, like eating a pomegranate
he wrote down his rulings as law

test.q: What does lifnim mishurat hadin mean?
choices: doing more than the strict rule requires
test.why: It means going inside the line of the law.

test.q: What happened to Rabbi Eliezer after the oven debate, in the story?
choices: the rabbis placed him under a ban
he became the leader of Yavneh
test.why: Bava Metzia 59b tells of the ban and tells it with sorrow.

test.q: Which pair are the last of the zugot?
test.why: Avot 1 ends the pairs with Hillel and Shammai.

choices: returning or turning from a wrong
test.why: Teshuvah is the rabbinic path of repair.

write.prompt: Can people disagree strongly and still show mercy? Use two or three passages from this unit, such as Eruvin 13b, Bava Metzia 59b, Bava Metzia 58b or Mishnah Avot 1:14. Explain what each passage says and how its readers have understood it.
tips: Name the tractate and page for every passage you use.
Attribute each idea: 'the Gemara says', 'Hillel teaches', 'readers have argued'.
Compare readings; do not judge any tradition.
Use at least three of the unit's words.
Keep minority views in view, as the Talmud does.
